Julius Caesar's own account of his conquest of Gaul, in Latin Commentarii de Bello Gallico. Seven books cover each year from 58 to 52 BCE; an eighth was added by his officer Aulus Hirtius.

It opens with the famous line "All Gaul is divided into three parts." Caesar writes about himself in the third person, as "Caesar", in plain, clear Latin. Cicero praised its bare style. It reads like a soldier's report, but it was also political publicity: it showed Romans at home a brave, careful general fighting for Rome's safety, while Caesar's enemies in the Senate were trying to bring him down.

It is our main source for the Gallic Wars, for Vercingetorix, and for Gaul itself. Caesar describes the tribes, their nobles, and the druids, and he sets Gauls against the wilder Germans across the Rhine, a contrast Tacitus took up later.

He also wrote a sequel, the Civil War. For centuries the Gallic War was the first real Latin book that schoolchildren read.
sum: Julius Caesar's own account of his conquest of Gaul, in Latin Commentarii de Bello Gallico. Seven books cover each year from 58 to 52 BCE; an eighth was added by his officer Aulus Hirtius.
